program_name: Local Government Special Needs Housing Program (SNHP)
administering_agency: California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA), with county MHSA funds
typical_award_size: Historically county-funded MHSA capital loans and capitalized operating subsidies administered by CalHFA (16 participating counties as of 2019).
affordability_requirement: Permanent supportive housing units for persons with serious mental illness eligible for MHSA services.
layering_notes: No live CalHFA program page exists; the CalHFA multifamily programs page (source) no longer lists SNHP, and a DHCS notice (BH-IN-19-047) states CalHFA discontinued the program effective Jan 3, 2020 with county MHSA funds reverting to county control. Marked needs_confirmation because the DHCS notice could not be opened this pass. Successor supportive housing capital now comes from Homekey+, HCD MHP supportive units, and county Behavioral Health Services Act (Prop 1) housing allocations (research in Pass 2). CTCAC still lists SNHP commitments as qualifying homeless-assistance funding in the nonprofit set-aside.

program_name: Sonoma County Homeless Coalition (CoC CA-504) funding: HUD CoC competition and Homeless Services Consolidated NOFA (HHAP, ESG, HHIP)
administering_agency: Sonoma County Department of Health Services, Homelessness Services Division, as CoC collaborative applicant
typical_award_size: 2026 HUD CoC competition: about $4.9M in renewal funding; HUD had not announced CoC Bonus or DV Bonus amounts; local applications due July 21, 2026. Annual Homeless Services Consolidated NOFA (state ESG, one-time HHAP, DHCS HHIP and local sources): about $5.5M expected in the 2025-26 cycle (applications due Feb 7, 2025). HHAP rounds 1 to 5 brought $32.2M to the Sonoma area; HHAP Round 5 allowed one CoC Builds PSH construction project.
affordability_requirement: Homeless households via Coordinated Entry; CoC PSH rental assistance and services; HHAP permits permanent housing capital as an eligible use.
layering_notes: Operating-side partner for PSH: CoC rental assistance or HHAP operating subsidy can replace or supplement PBVs on supportive units. HHAP capital for permanent housing is allowed but Sonoma has directed most HHAP to shelter, outreach and rehousing. Developers should engage the Homelessness Services Division early so a PSH project appears in the CoC's regional action plan and Coordinated Entry referral agreements.

program_name: Napa County Affordable ADU Forgivable Loan Program (single-unit, recorded for completeness)
administering_agency: Napa County Housing and Community Services
typical_award_size: Under the updated underwriting guidelines (V2) adopted by the Board on March 10, 2026: base forgivable loan $60,000 for a 1-bedroom or $85,000 for a 2-bedroom ADU plus up to $20,000 in rebates, for a total maximum of $80,000 or $105,000 (lesser of that amount or actual development cost). 5.0% simple deferred interest, forgiven monthly (1/60) over the 5-year affordability term; opt-out by repaying the unforgiven balance. Launched March 2023 (2023 range was $45,000 to $105,000). Funded from the Affordable Housing Fund.
affordability_requirement: Owner-occupant of a single-family home in Napa County rents the ADU to a household at or below 80% AMI at HCD 80% AMI rents (2026 examples $2,563 for 1-bedroom, $2,884 for 2-bedroom) under a 5-year covenant; loan forgiven on compliance.
layering_notes: Not a multifamily source; recorded so the Affordable Housing Fund's competing uses are visible (ADU loans, farmworker centers, homeless services and fair housing all draw on the same fee revenue). Terms from the Napa Valley Community Foundation launch notice (March 17, 2023) and County news releases quoted in search results; napacounty.gov pages and DocumentCenter PDFs sit behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06, so the county's own page could not be opened; the 2026 notice is https://www.napacounty.gov/CivicAlerts.aspx?AID=858.

program_name: Behavioral Health Services Act Integrated Plan FY 2026-29: housing interventions, capital development and operating subsidies
administering_agency: Fresno County Department of Behavioral Health (Integrated Plan approved by the Board June 16, 2026)
typical_award_size: Housing Interventions component expenditures: $26,929,779 (FY 2026-27), $30,078,356 (FY 2027-28), $31,885,245 (FY 2028-29). Capital development $6,098,789 to $6,118,094 a year (24.8% of the component in year one, under the 25% cap), permanent rental subsidies $7,092,044 plus bundled rental and operating $2,526,608, interim rental subsidies $1,207,577 and bundled $2,250,773, outreach $1,709,758, participant assistance $373,266, Housing Flex Pool start-up $400,000 a year, flex pool share rising from 50% to 80%. First capital commitment: Victory Village (959 N. Parkway Drive, Fresno; Fresno Housing conversion of a shelter to 42 units, 41 PSH for chronically homeless) conditional $6,300,000 capital plus $287,000 a year operating subsidy for 30 years ($8,610,000) and on-site services valued at $424,872 a year, contingent on 2026 Round 2 9% tax credits (resolution June 30, 2026).
affordability_requirement: BHSA eligible adults with serious mental illness or substance use disorder; at least 50% of housing funds for chronically homeless people; Victory Village carries a 30-year use restriction for 41 PSH units.
layering_notes: Fresno County splits housing work three ways: the Department of Public Works and Planning, Community Development Division (ComDev) runs the Urban County HUD programs, PLHA and the annual Affordable Housing Development NOFO; the County Administrative Office's new Office of Housing and Homelessness (OHH, created November 18, 2025) administers HHAP, the Continuum of Care and Transitional Rent and is absorbing housing programs from Behavioral Health and ComDev (Phase 2 approved November 3, 2026); and the Department of Behavioral Health co-applies for Homekey+ and NPLH and funds BHSA housing. Fresno Housing (the joint City and County Housing Authorities) is the dominant developer and voucher source. The City of Fresno and Clovis are separate entitlements with their own programs (Pass 3). fresnocountyca.gov and fresnohousing.org open normally; Board records are on fresnocounty.legistar.com and the Legistar web API client 'fresnocounty'. Fresno is one of the few counties in this database putting BHSA into capital (about $6.1 million a year) and into long operating subsidies ($287,000 a year for 30 years at Victory Village, $15.3 million over 20 years at Sendero Commons). Tenant-based subsidies serve 869 people in year one rising to 1,049, 372 units a year. Capital money has gone first to Fresno Housing (Victory Village) and to the Homekey+ project in Sanger. Source is the revised 2026-2029 Integrated Plan PDF; budget figures from the Integrated Plan Budget attachment to Board file 26-0538 and the Victory Village resolution (file 26-0585). Audit 2026-11-08: classed as grant because the BHSA Integrated Plan funds housing capital (Capital Development Projects $6,098,789 to $6,118,094 a year) and rental and operating subsidies for housing; the Victory Village resolution (No. 26-251) is a conditional capital commitment and operating subsidy, and the loan or grant form of the capital will be set in the enforceable funding agreement after a 9% award.

program_name: Behavioral Health Services Act Integrated Plan FY 2026-29 (Housing Interventions component)
administering_agency: Ventura County Health Care Agency, Behavioral Health Department
typical_award_size: DHCS-approved BHSA Integrated Plan FY 2026-29 (May 2026) funds Housing Interventions: rental subsidies (706 people per year, 620 units, project-based and tenant-based), operating subsidies for PSH and interim settings (355 units per year), landlord mitigation and participant assistance funds, and capital development (up to 25% of Housing Interventions). Named capital projects with BHSA cost per unit: Santa Paula Motel Project (20 BHSA units of 21, $150,712 per unit, leasing 2028), Santa Clara Apartments (10 BHSA units, $213,538 per unit, leasing summer 2029), Fillmore Terrace (4 BHSA units, $200,000 per unit, leasing early 2029). Annual dollar totals are in a separate budget template not posted as an accessible file.
affordability_requirement: BHSA-eligible adults and youth with serious mental illness or substance use disorder, including chronically homeless individuals; referrals through Coordinated Entry and HMIS.
layering_notes: BHSA classified as grant because the Integrated Plan funds housing capital development, operating subsidies and rental subsidies for PSH. Capital projects braid BHSA with LIHTC, NPLH, HHAP and other sources. The Plan says VCBH is not participating in a Flex Pool at this time, so the earlier note about RFP 226001 for a Flexible Housing Subsidy Pool operator was not confirmed. Behavioral Health Bridge Housing capacity will be partly sustained with BHSA funds. Ventura County housing funding otherwise runs through CEO Community Development (CDBG, HOME Consortium, PLHA), the Area Housing Authority and the Housing Trust Fund Ventura County.

program_name: Behavioral Health Services Act Integrated Plan FY 2026-29 (Housing Interventions component)
administering_agency: Merced County Behavioral Health and Recovery Services
typical_award_size: 2026-2029 BHSA Three-Year Integrated Plan, adopted by the Board June 2, 2026: Housing Interventions get 30% of the allocation ($6,900,000 base; $7,103,217 per year including MHSA funds). Year-one budget: $5,825,678 bundled rental and operating subsidies in permanent settings, $349,189 interim rental subsidies, $40,800 interim operating subsidies, $25,000 interim bundled subsidies, $711,546 for one capital development project (a County interim and peer respite site, 4 units and 6 beds, no braided non-BHSA funds, cost about $118,591 per unit, available July 1, 2027), plus landlord mitigation and participant assistance funds. The plan also notes County No Place Like Home capital funds for a Homekey+ project and partnerships on Mercy Village and 1213 V Street.
affordability_requirement: BHSA eligible adults and youth with serious mental illness or substance use disorder; at least half of housing funds for chronically homeless people.
layering_notes: Classed grant because the BHSA plan funds rental and operating subsidies for housing and a small capital project. The FY 2026-29 plan budgets about $5.8 million a year in bundled rental and operating subsidies for permanent settings, which a PSH developer could pair with Coordinated Entry referrals; the only BHSA capital project is a County-run interim and peer respite site, and PSH capital has come from No Place Like Home (Homekey+ project). Development partners named in the plan: Community Holdings or Upholdings (Mercy Village, 1213 V Street), Central Valley Coalition for Affordable Housing and Richmond Properties (the Retreat). The County BHSA page and plan PDF opened directly on November 8, 2026.

program_name: Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) Housing Interventions, 2026-2029 Integrated Plan
typical_award_size: Three-year BHSA Integrated Plan (FY 2026/27 to 2028/29), approved by the Board of Supervisors June 2, 2026 (Resolution 26-231); staff report estimates BHSA expenditures of $27,502,891 over three years. Housing Interventions base allocation is 30 percent: $2,460,099 (FY 26/27), $2,596,276 (FY 27/28) and $2,752,206 (FY 28/29), half for chronic homelessness. The County will use housing funds for rental subsidies (about 200 people a year, 103 in permanent supportive housing and 97 in interim hotel or motel stays), project-based and tenant-based, plus outreach and engagement; it will not use BHSA for capital development (0 of the allowed 25 percent). BHSA-funded PSH beds grew from 20 (2019) to 94 (2026), with about 24 Homekey+ units coming.
affordability_requirement: BHSA-eligible adults with serious mental illness or substance use disorder experiencing or at risk of homelessness; BHSA is the funding source of last resort for PSH.
layering_notes: Classified grant: the BHSA plan funds rental subsidies for permanent supportive housing (project-based and tenant-based), not capital. Nevada County's Housing and Community Services Department (HCS) administers the Western Nevada County Regional Housing Trust Fund, PLHA, state HOME and CDBG awards and the Down Payment Assistance Program; the Behavioral Health Department holds Homekey+, BHSA and the Truckee Navigation Center; HHAP is administered by the Homeless Resource Council of the Sierras (CoC CA-531); the Regional Housing Authority supplies vouchers. BHSA rental assistance is used where a voucher is not available, so a PSH developer should plan on BHSA as an operating or rental subsidy source for a handful of units, not as gap capital. Capital has come from BHBH, BHCIP, ERF and Homekey+ instead. Staff report and resolution are on Legistar (nevco matter SR 26-0325).

program_name: Affordable housing land dedication sites under Article 18.05 (Village Farms 16-acre dedication, Project Individualized Plan Exhibit E)
administering_agency: City of Davis Community Development Department and Social Services and Housing Department (Council subcommittee negotiates development agreements)
typical_award_size: Land, not cash. Village Farms Davis (Development Agreement Exhibit E, approved December 16, 2025 and revised January 13, 2026) dedicates 16 acres to the City for 280 low and very low income units on fully improved sites (no more than 4 parcels, none under 2.5 acres), to be developed with a qualified affordable housing developer selected by the City, with the City to endeavor to add 80 moderate income units. Baseline features now require construction to commence on 100 affordable units before Phase 3 and no permits beyond the first 150 until that starts; the City holds an option after 150 units. Together with the $6 million Housing Trust Fund payment the package is valued by the applicant at over $6 million plus land.
affordability_requirement: 280 low and very low income units (plus up to 80 moderate) on dedicated land; affordability covenants set in the City's developer agreement.
layering_notes: This is how 100% affordable developers get sites in Davis: the inclusionary ordinance's land dedication option plus Housing Trust Fund money, then compete for 9% credits, MHP, AHSC or HCD Super NOFA money. Vice Mayor Vaitla's December 2025 direction to amend the land dedication option (so dedicators also provide resources) led to a March 2026 ordinance introduction, so later projects should carry cash with the land. Earlier dedications (Cannery, Chiles Ranch, Bretton Woods) produced sites now built or in pipeline. Davis has no city-owned surplus land program beyond these dedications. Pair with Yolo County Housing PBVs and the CoC HHAP money for supportive units.

program_name: City-owned land for affordable housing: 505 Royer Street and 300 Taylor Street sale to Eden Housing (Resolution 26-331, September 16, 2026)
administering_agency: City of Roseville Economic Development Department (Gina McColl, 916-774-5452) with the Housing Division
typical_award_size: Land sale at appraised value rather than a grant: two parcels totaling 1.17 acres in the Downtown Specific Plan (former Placer County courthouse site, demolished 2021, declared surplus October 23, 2019) sold to Eden Housing for $580,000 after a May 2025 RFP (Eden was the sole respondent) for a 58-unit senior affordable project at 30% to 60% AMI. A prior 2022 contract with Bridge Housing for a similar project was terminated in September 2024 for lack of financing. Escrow closes no later than January 31, 2027; construction estimated January 2030. Eden also applied for the City's 2026 PIP NOFA for this site but was not selected.
affordability_requirement: Senior affordable housing for lower-income households (30% to 60% AMI) per Eden's proposal; regulatory agreement terms to be set with City financing.
layering_notes: Shows Roseville's practice of running Surplus Land Act and RFP processes for infill sites and pairing them with LHTF or PIP loans and CDBG. The Eden project will still need County gap money (Placer County in-lieu fee loans or Housing Trust Placer), RHA or PCHA PBVs and LIHTC. Read from the September 16, 2026 agenda packet via the CivicClerk API.

program_name: Capitola Affordable Housing Trust Fund (established November 2004) and Affordable Housing Impact Fee ($25 per square foot, adopted 2021)
administering_agency: City of Capitola Community and Economic Development Department ((831) 475-7300)
typical_award_size: Trust fund balance about $144,000 (2023-2031 Housing Element, certified August 2024); revenue to date has come only from inclusionary in-lieu fees, with donations allowed. Uses: matching funds for state and federal sources, acquisition of units for affordable resale, and gap assistance; no loan guidelines, per-project limit or NOFA are adopted. Affordable Housing Impact Fee: $25 per square foot on new market-rate residential development, including multifamily rental, adopted in 2021 after a nexus study (the earlier schedule was $6 per square foot on rental projects, $10 per square foot in-lieu on for-sale projects and $2.50 per square foot on additions); exemptions or waivers for deed-restricted affordable units are not stated on the pages opened. PLHA: state estimate of $630,557 for Capitola over the 2020-2024 cycle, application pending at the time the Housing Element was written. Capitola imposes no park, transportation, administration or childcare exactions; school fees ($4.08 per square foot) and Central Fire District fees ($0.53 per square foot) apply.
affordability_requirement: Trust fund monies are directed to new low and very low income units (Section 18.02.050) and to affordable units for moderate income and below; the impact fee is used exclusively to facilitate affordable housing development.
layering_notes: Capitola's fund is too small (about $144,000) to serve as gap financing; its value is as a local match or fee offset in a TCAC or HCD application, with capital from the County's Chapter 17.10 AHIF fund being unavailable inside city limits. The $25 per square foot impact fee is a significant cost on market-rate rental projects (the County charges $2 per habitable square foot on rentals), so mixed-income sponsors should model it; the fee feasibility analysis (EPS, 2021) warned rental development was marginal even before the increase. Density increases are available under the mixed-use AHO successor provisions for 20% lower income units (record below). Sources opened: 2023-2031 Housing Element PDF (DocumentCenter 1797), 2021 fee feasibility analysis (DocumentCenter 699) and the March 23, 2026 Annual Progress Report memo. Audit reclassification: funding_type set to loan because Housing Element Program 2.7 states the City uses the Housing Trust Fund to provide loans and grants (Housing Rehabilitation Loan and Grant Program, feasibility studies, and permanent financing of acquisition-rehab and new construction affordable projects); the balance is only about $144,000. The Housing Element also states a $6 per square foot impact fee for multifamily rental housing alongside the $25 per square foot fee, so confirm the rental rate with the City.

administering_agency: City of Atwater as Housing and Non-Housing Successor Agency
typical_award_size: Unknown. The City elected to be the housing successor, but the successor agency page lists only 2012-2015 ROPS and oversight board documents. No current SB 341 report or fund balance was found.
